en: Preface to the *Tunhai Ji* (Collection on Swallowing the Sea) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*,
compiled by Ma Bu-jun, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness of the Left, Director of the Dragon Diagram Pavilion,
Administrator of the Military Prefecture of Jingnan, and Supervisor of the Public Affairs of the Jinghu Bei Road Pacification Command.
Written by Tao Kai, Concurrent Commissioner for Irrigation and Agriculture:

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* of the Buddha contains the causes and effects, the stages of practice, the conditions of arising, and the principles and phenomena. It takes the inconceivable as its central tenet;
it is the Vehicle of the Supreme. While it is identical [in essence], it horizontally opens up hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates; yet its totality is non-dual.
It is the same, yet it is taken as different; yet when one returns to the ground of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), their distinction is not other than identity.

Thus, they are both identical and different, and the principle reaches its ultimate point in this harmony. Therefore, within identity there is difference: like birds soaring through the sky, their before and after are simultaneously revealed.

Within difference there is identity: like waves arising from water, they merge into a single, undifferentiated unity. All phenomena each abide in their own position, like water and fire that do not intermingle.
Extinction and non-extinction do not coexist; yet the ultimate principle is not separated by even a hair’s breadth.
It is as if dust and chaff are contained within one another without any obstruction—a state that cannot be communicated through the phenomenal world nor reached by the power of conceptual thought.

Nevertheless, there are no words by which to clarify its meaning, and no phrases by which to constitute its expression; thus, they are interwoven and elegantly threaded together to form this composition.

Spread out, they are divided like the stars; this is why this scripture is called a "sūtra. If one seeks it through words, phrases, and names, then while every dharma resembles every other dharma, each stage (bhūmi) possesses its own distinctions.
Their multiplicity is counted in the hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions, even to the point of being incalculable, yet they have not escaped being within the realm of number.
As for their vastness, they encompass the ten directions and the three periods of time.
It is measured, even to the point of being immeasurable, yet it has not transcended the realm of the measurable.
As for a sutra being a sutra, since it relies upon words and phrases, its profundity cannot exceed this.

When taking that which is supremely vast and inexhaustible in the world, one uses the ocean as a metaphor—namely, the so-called "ten oceans," such as the worlds, sentient beings, and the karmic retributions of all Buddhas.

The Dharma-realm, the faculties, desires, wheels of Dharma, vows, powers, spiritual transformations, and Buddha-emanations are all the ultimate karmic products of the Buddhas, forming an ocean of identical names.
Within this, the seven locations, nine assemblies, and thirty-nine chapters are all its waves; none can emerge from it.
Its source has no beginning, its current has no end, its boundaries have no periphery, and its depths have no bottom. Thus, one takes it as the ocean.
This is taken as a metaphor. Is this not the ultimate description under heaven?

Yet when one seeks it within the realm of heaven and earth—among forms and vessels—that which can embody the principle of integration and fit perfectly in every detail is perhaps none other than the sea. This is the meaning of the scripture.
The practice of [translating] in China began with the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty. Its texts are vast and extensive; its meanings are profound and subtle; its Way is grand and expansive.
Those of inferior resolve grow weary at the abundance of its cataloged volumes; those of shallow intelligence are bewildered by the subtlety of its purport;

and those of narrow capacity are startled by the ultimate nature of its fruition. It is already difficult to find anyone capable of merely reciting its texts, let alone one who can fully comprehend its meaning.
Furthermore, as for practicing this Way: it is like a single object within the ocean that is itself contained by the ocean;
how could it possibly encompass the ocean within its own measure? From the Yixi era until now, several thousand years have passed.

Among the commentaries and exegeses currently in circulation, there are only those of the Venerable Zao Bo’s *Treatise* and Master Qingliang’s *Commentary*; their explanations are increasingly expansive. —Yantai Tonglao.
The Dharma Master attained the Avataṃsaka Samādhi. Although he received his training from a teacher, he brought his own mind to full realization.

He could expand upon a single phrase into ten thousand words, yet condense an entire chapter into just a few sentences. When one savors his ten-thousand-word expositions in detail, not a single word is superfluous;
when one seeks out the meaning of his few-sentence summaries, not a single point is lacking. Thus he calculated:

Without waiting for enumeration, people perceive its multiplicity; without needing measurement, people recognize its vastness. The dharmas follow their sequence according to the stages (bhūmi), without being confused or intermingled.
It is as if they are manifested beyond the words and phrases, yet they sport within them, ultimately remaining unbound by characters, words, or names.
Taking these concise explanations, they have been transmitted to the world, totaling ten thousand [verses].
It consists of several thousand words and is titled *Tunhai* (Swallowing the Sea). How could the sea be swallowed? The multitude will surely regard this as a fabrication.
However, there is a principle by which it can be swallowed: one who is capable of creating the sea. Master Tong’s *Yueshuo* (Concise Discourse) is likewise merely a matter of words and phrases;

how could it involve the creation of the sea? What I mean by "ultimately not being bound by words and phrases" is that the student must unravel the meaning of the text and apply it [to their own realization].
Reflect upon this, and you shall surely attain it. Alas! A great thousand-fold world-system scripture may be covered by a single speck of dust;
only the wise can extract it from there. The Dharma-ocean of the *Avataṃsaka* may be swallowed in a single gulp without leaving a single drop behind;
only those who know the Way can believe in it. Whether emerging or entering, how could these be external? They occur within the mere interval of one’s own inhalation and exhalation.
Preface to the *Tunhai Ji* (Collection on Swallowing the Sea) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*,
spoken by the Dharma-heir Bhikṣu Daotong, who has transmitted the lineages of the *Avataṃsaka*, *Śūraṅgama*, *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda* Śāstras.
I humbly observe that as for the teaching of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, it is the ultimate source to which all other scriptures converge;

and as for the commentary of Qingliang [Zongmi], it illuminates and surpasses all that came before. Were it not for Xingda, who could have elucidated these works? Daotong has long attached himself to the True Vehicle and dwells in seclusion within the lecture halls.

I have listened to the discourses on the benefits [of the teachings] and studied the sutras that transmit the wondrous emptiness. Yet, I am humbled by comparison to the sages of old and find myself of no benefit to future students.

Having spent ten years in inquiry and expounded [the teachings] three times, I have repeatedly endured hardships and illnesses, which have caused my faculties to decline even further. I have built a hermitage on Mount Lu to merely prolong my days.
Yet, two or three scholars have still not abandoned me, daily engaging with me in discussions regarding this scripture.
Taking the *Avataṃsaka* as my primary concern, I perused an old chest and recovered the Dharma-meanings I had compiled, titled "Swallowing the Sea.

I offer this to the talented youths of later generations, so that within each and every category they may perceive the inexhaustible sutras, and within every atom they may suddenly behold the vastness of the Flower Treasury Ocean at the tip of a single hair.
Extensive! How could it be said that this is but a small supplement? To know without learning is impossible; I have heard his words, but I have not yet seen the man himself.
May those who share my heart not reproach me for this.
The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra: The Collection of the Swallowing of the Sea, Volume One.
Composed by Daotong of the Plain of He-shuo. Chapter One:
The Assembly at the Site of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa).
First is the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Lord.
Within this scripture, there are three types of worlds: first, the world of the perfectly awakened through wisdom (*jñāna-saṃbuddha-loka*), whose lord is the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha;

second, the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), whose lords are human kings and celestial kings; third, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), whose lords are the various classes of deities. If one is able...
When the primary and secondary realms are mutually interfused, then the inconceivable objects are all equally wondrous adornments.
This means that while the world-rulers possess differentiated characteristics, their wondrous adornments share a single, equal essence. Thus, they are the wondrous adornments of the world-rulers.
Sentient beings possess the virtues of a Buddha; if they are the Sovereign Lord (Lokanātha), they are the Sublime Adornment (Sudhana).

The virtues of a Buddha depend upon sentient beings; if the Sovereign Lord is the Sublime Adornment, this Dharma is equal. If the Sublime Adornment is the Sovereign Lord, then the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.
If one possesses these four propositions, one accomplishes the virtues of a Buddha; if one dissolves these four propositions, they become daily function. If...
Existence and extinction are unimpeded; the living and the Buddha are equal. Such is the nature of the Dharma; there is no need for laborious cultivation or realization. Thus it is.

First, the Hīnayāna, which distinguishes itself from non-Buddhist paths through the *āgama* sūtras. Second, the Initial Teaching, consisting of words of faith and compliance. Third, the Final Teaching:
"Suchness" (*tathatā*) refers to its unchanging nature, while "is" (*iti*) refers to its following conditions. Fourth, the Sudden Teaching: only Suchness is taken as the standard.
This refers to the five teachings. First, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): like a sheath that is all-pervasive. Second, the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna):

it holds that sound exists outside of consciousness. Third, the Initial Teaching (Shijiao): it holds that the appearance of sound is a transformation of consciousness, which is conventionally designated as "self."

Third is the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao): purity and self are such that the sounds and objects of the senses are immediately the mind. Fourth is the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao): there is no self, as both faculties and objects are completely exhausted.
Fifth is the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): hearing one thing is hearing all things.
First, the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) has six periods of day and night. Second, the Initial Teaching (Ādikarmika-yāna): time manifests based on consciousness. Third, the Final Teaching (Niṣṭhā-yāna):
that which is unchanging follows conditions. Fourth, the Sudden Teaching (Aksipya-yāna): Prajñā manifests before one. Fifth, the Perfect Teaching (Pūrṇa-yāna):
all times are possessed simultaneously.
The Buddha exists in five ways: first, in the Hinayana, as the six-foot true body; second, in the Initial Teaching, as the thousand-billion transformation bodies;
third, in the Final Teaching, where the six-foot body is itself the eternal body; fourth, in the Sudden Teaching, where the six-foot body is itself the Dharma-body;
and fifth, in the Perfect Teaching, wherein he is fully endowed with the ten bodies.

1. The Bodhi tree represents the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna). 2. The various mountains of earth and stone represent the Initial Teaching (Ādikarmika-yāna), which manifests traces of transformation according to the capacities of beings.

3. The firmness of the ground represents the Final Teaching (Nisthā-yāna). 4. The non-establishment of even a single atom represents the Sudden Teaching (Aksipya-yāna). 5. The seven locations and nine assemblies being a single site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) represents the Perfect Teaching (Pūrṇa-yāna).
1. The assembly of Bodhisattvas; 2. The Hīnayāna, which neither sees nor hears [this]; 3. The Initial Teaching (Shijiao), which has forty-two stages; 4.

The Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), in which all attain Buddhahood; 5. The Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao), in which there is neither ordinary person nor sage; 6. The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), where those as numerous as the atoms of Buddha-lands gather together.

In the sutra, it is said that when Śākyamuni Tathāgata first attained Buddhahood, he was already fully endowed with the ten bodies inherent from the beginning and had realized perfect enlightenment regarding all dharmas. The meaning is this:

"initially attaining perfect enlightenment" refers to a primordial Buddha newly manifesting his realization. As for "sitting upon this seat," it refers to [the manifestation of] the opening [of the teaching].
The locus of awakening is equal in measure to the *dharmadhātu* and like empty space; it possesses the two meanings of universal pervasiveness and vast capacity.
The syllogism states: The subject is that the three karmas of the Tathāgata possess a dharma of correct and constant pervasion. The reason is that they are equal and non-discriminative.
For example, just as empty space equally enters into all lands, when even a single atom serves as a seat, [the entire universe is contained therein].
He attains equal and perfect enlightenment. If he takes a single hair as his seat, he then turns the Great Wheel of Dharma, surrounded by Bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust;
thus, the principal and the retinue mutually adorn one another.
In the sutra, the assembly is enumerated from the inner to the outer, and the Buddha’s virtues are praised in verse.
From Maheśvara down to the ocean-like clouds of Samantabhadra, there are twenty types of assemblies born together with the Tathāgata:
from Samantabhadra to the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi, and from Sāgaraprabha to the Bodhisattva Jñānasaṃbhava. There are ten types of assemblies of those born separately, who hold... [text ends].
The Vajra deity; the deity of the body hosts; the deity of foot-travelers; the deity of the site of enlightenment; the deity presiding over cities; the deity presiding over the earth;

the deity presiding over mountains; the deity presiding over forests; the deity presiding over medicinal herbs; the deity presiding over crops; the deity presiding over rivers; and the deity presiding over the ocean.
The Lord of the Water Devas; the Lord of the Fire Devas; the Lord of the Wind Devas; the Lord of the Space Devas; the Lord of the Directional Devas;
the Lord of the Night Devas; the Lord of the Day Devas; the Asura King; the Garuḍa King;
the Kiṃnara King; the Mahoraga King; the Yakṣa King; the Nāga King; the Kumbhāṇḍa King; the Gandharva King; the Moon Devaputra; and the Sun [Devaputra].
The Son of Heaven; the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the Yāma Heaven; the Tuṣita Heaven; the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven;
the Mahābrahmā Heaven; the Ābhāsvara Heaven; the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; the Bṛhatphala Heaven; and the Maheśvara Heaven.
In the sutra, the assembly is enumerated from the inner to the outer, while the verses praising the Buddha’s virtues proceed from the outer to the inner.
There are as many Vairocana Buddhas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, each surrounded by a retinue of sixty assemblies;
their forms, colors, and categories are each distinct, yet they have attained the equality of the Buddha’s liberation, which is non-dual.
Second is the Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Manifestation of Signs.
In the *Sūtra on the Rituals for Preaching the Dharma*, the Buddha emits light from between his eyebrows; it circumambulates the Buddha to the right and enters through his feet.
A great lotus flower suddenly appears, and the Bodhisattva Varaghoṣa sits upon the lotus and praises the Tathāgata with verses.
There were ten bodhisattvas as companions. [The Master] thought:
"In the realm of the principle of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), neither host nor guest is established; yet within the gate of arising and ceasing, how could there not be questions and answers?
The Bodhisattvas and the various kings reflected thus: from cause to fruit, there are forty questions in this one section.
The scriptural passage states that, in order to sever those doubts, the Buddha emitted ten kinds of light rays from between his teeth in his face.
All the bodhisattvas, having received the Buddha’s light, went to the Tathāgata’s presence to attend upon and make offerings to him.

Chapter Three: The Samādhi of Samantabhadra. It is stated in the sutra that one does not speak [of this] without having attained realization. Therein, Samantabhadra beholds the Buddha manifesting signs;

empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he enters the Tathāgata-garbha-kāya-samādhi, which is equal to empty space. Within every single atom, there are oceans of worlds and Buddhas. One by one...

Before the Buddha was Samantabhadra, who had entered this samādhi. At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared before him and bestowed upon Samantabhadra ten kinds of wisdom for expounding the Dharma. Each extended their right hand and stroked the crown of Samantabhadra’s head.
This occurred in the same manner within every single atom. When he arose from one samādhi, he immediately arose from all samādhis.
Arising from the gateway of profound illumination, one attains all the dharmas of the ocean-clouds. All worlds in the ten directions tremble.
This is the Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Four Worlds.
Throughout the general scriptures of the sages, it is taught that the Ocean of Worlds possesses ten matters, and likewise, the Ocean of Sentient Beings possesses ten matters. According to this...
One knows that for each of the oceans of Buddhas, there are ten matters, such as their arising, their equipment, their causes and conditions, their basis, and their dwelling.
For each matter, there is first a prose section followed by a verse. One ocean has these ten matters; ten oceans have one hundred matters.
The commentary states: First, one contemplates the inexhaustible realm, and then explains the inexhaustible Dharma. All sentient beings are fundamentally and fully endowed with it.
The "Chapter on the Five Flower-Treasury Worlds" specifically reveals the original teacher.
In the sutras, it is specifically explained that the adornments and purifications of the Original Teacher are like rows of teeth set upright in the mouths of geese, or like inverted pagodas;
within these, the various worlds each abide according to their respective locations and possess their respective forms.
Each has its own essential nature, each its own adornment, and each its own arrangement, numbering twenty tiers.
From outside this central Great Lotus World, proceeding clockwise from that point, one speaks of a hundred sets of twenty-tiered worlds—ten unspeakable world-systems.
One should understand by analogy that all of these exist entirely within a single mote of dust.
Chapter Six: Vairocana. In the sutras concerning the cultivation of causes in the past, the cultivation of causes was vast and the attainment of the fruit was infinite.

Because Samantabhadra’s exposition encompasses both cause and fruit, it is said that in ages long past, during the eon of Jyotirghoṣa (Victorious Sound), to the east of the Great Forest of Maṇipuṣpamañjaricakra (Jewel Flower Branch Wheel).
The Great City of Blazing Light is the capital of the King of Men, surrounded by ten billion cities.
It has one hundred trillion gates, and before each gate stand forty-nine jeweled *śīla*-banners. The inhabitants of the city travel through the air;
whatever they desire arrives according to their thought. The celestial cities and dragon cities revolve clockwise around it.
Arranged in rows within the Forest of Flower Branches was the Universal Illumination Bodhimanda.
There, the Buddha Supreme Sound of Mount Sumeru of All Merits suddenly appeared; his body was all-pervasive, equal to the true Dharma-realm.
Prince Great Majestic Light, beholding the Buddha’s radiance, attained ten kinds of dharmas and praised the Buddha’s virtues in verse, departing from the City of Blazing Light.

A multitude of hundreds of billions mounted into the air and traveled there together to see the Buddha. That Buddha preached for them the *Sūtra on the Universal Collection of the Sovereign Dharmas of the Buddhas of the Three Times*.
The Bodhisattva Great Majestic Radiance attained the realization that all dharmas entirely enter the initial mind of enlightenment.
That Buddha lived for five billion years after receiving his mandate; following the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha—
There was a Buddha named Suvilocana-pāramitā who attained equal and perfect enlightenment within a great forest.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahātejas immediately attained the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi called Anantodadhinidhānamegha. That Buddha preached for him the *Dharmadhātusvabhāva-viśuddhi-sūtra*;
having heard it, he obtained pure wisdom. When that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, [the Bodhisattva] continued his practice.
King Priyadarśana also passed away shortly thereafter. The Bodhisattva Mahātejas succeeded him to the position of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
In that great forest, a third Buddha appeared, named Guṇasāgaravara.
From this Buddha, Mahātejas heard the exposition of the *Sūtra on the Practice of Universal Eye Radiance* and attained the samādhi of Great Merit. In that great forest...
Furthermore, there was a Buddha who appeared named Universal Renown Lotus-Eye Great Majestic Radiance.
Having passed away from this life, he was reborn on the summit of Mount Sumeru as the Great Heavenly King named Stainless Merit Banner.
The Tathāgata preached the *Sūtra of Vast Expedient Means* for him, whereby he attained the Samādhi of the Universal Gate’s Joyful Treasury.
The Master said: "During the Kalpa of Supreme Sound, there appeared as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten Mount Sumerus.
The Bodhisattva Great Majestic Light made offerings to each one of them, heard their sutras, and attained the Dharma; because of this, his merit is inexhaustible."
Now there are ten unspeakable world-systems; these fruits are infinite.
Second is the "Chapter on the Names of the Seven Tathāgatas" from the *Universal Radiance Hall Assembly*, concerning the pervasiveness of the physical body (*kāyakarman*).
In the sutra, it is said that his wondrous realization is fully perfected and the two types of conduct are forever severed; thus twenty-one kinds of the Buddha’s merits are extolled.
If the World-Honored One would take pity on us, he should reveal the ten questions regarding the causes and the thirty questions regarding the fruits.
The World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, manifested supernatural powers. The Bodhisattva Ten Heads arrived at the Hall of Universal Radiance and thought:
"In the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, faith is the primary prerequisite. A follower of the Small Vehicle believes only in the Buddha alone."
1. Attaining the Way (the Hīnayāna). 2. The Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna: believing that one portion and a half of sentient beings will not attain Buddhahood.
3. The Final Teaching: believing that one’s own nature is determined to attain Buddhahood. 4. The Sudden Teaching: believing that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is fundamentally non-existent.
5. The Perfect Teaching: neither attainment nor non-attainment; when one is attained, all are attained.
In the sutra, Mañjuśrī says: "The names and bodies of all Buddhas are inconceivable. One should not abide in the view of a single phenomenon as being the name and body of a Buddha.
Within this Sahā world, across the various four continents, the Tathāgata has various names and various bodies;
his physical marks, lifespan, locations, and assemblies are all diverse and different."
Within these four continents, he is known by such names as Sarvārthasiddha, Pūrṇacandra, Gautama, or Mahāśramaṇa.
In the eastern world-system, Sukhāvatī, he likewise has ten names;
each of the remaining nine world-systems also has ten names, totaling one hundred thousand names, which are able to bring benefit to the multitude.
Each person perceives it differently.
This means that the Buddha has inexhaustible names; whatever names the myriad phenomena throughout the world are established with, they are all names of the Buddha.
At this dwelling place, it may be called a lantern, or a table, or an incense burner, or...

It is called "emerald bamboo" or "yellow flowers. If one can apply the mind in this way to see the Buddha, then with every step one is the appearance of Śākyamuni in the world, and with every thought one is the descent of Maitreya. Thus, one perceives the Buddha-body pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Chapter Eighty-four: The Noble Truths. Verbal karma pervades the entire sūtra.
Suffering refers to the retribution within the three realms; accumulation refers to the causes within the three realms; cessation refers to transcending the three realms.

The Way consists of the causes of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom; it brings about the knowledge of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path.
It is the Buddha’s verbal activity, which tames sentient beings individually according to their respective minds. In the Sahā world, there are ten names for each of the Truths;
in the other nine worlds, there are likewise ten names for each of the Four Truths. Regarding the Truth of Suffering, they may be named as follows: [or named...]
It may be termed "loathsome," or "oppressive," or "impure. The meaning is this:
all names arise from causes and shift according to karmic functions; thus, names lack the power to grasp objects, and objects lack the reality to correspond to their names.
Yet, if one can use these provisional names to give rise to wholesome states, this is precisely the immeasurable verbal activity of the Transformation Buddha.
If one speaks of the Tathāgata’s lands and his physical and vocal actions, then the sound of wind bells and the songs of birds are all the voice of the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma.
When speech devoid of meaning expresses the non-dual dharma, one suddenly perceives the original mind and simultaneously transcends both existence and non-existence;
thus, one sees that the Buddha’s vocal action pervades the entire dharmadhātu.
Chapter Nine: The Awakening of the Nine Radiant Lights.

Regarding the mental karma that pervades the entire sūtra: the World-Honored One emitted light from between his two feet, illuminating this trichiliocosm, including ten billion Jambudvīpas, ten billion Cāturmahārājakāyika heavens, and so forth, up to ten billion Rūpadhātu realms.
The Ultimate Heaven (Akaniṣṭha). Within it, all things are clearly seen, surrounded by Bodhisattvas from the ten directions.

When a hundred billion Mañjuśrīs simultaneously raise their voices to praise the Buddha’s radiance, if one sees light being emitted that illuminates the ten directions and ten worlds, then there are ten hundred billion Mañjuśrīs praising the Buddha’s radiance. If one sees the emission of light...
When it passes beyond ten worlds, it illuminates a hundred worlds in the ten directions. Therein, thousands of billions of Mañjuśrīs praise the Buddha’s radiance.
If one sees the emission of light passing beyond a hundred worlds, it then illuminates a thousand worlds in the ten directions.
There were a hundred trillion Mañjuśrīs who praised the Buddha’s radiance: if he emitted light that passed beyond a hundred thousand worlds, it would illuminate a million;
if he emitted light that passed beyond a million, it would illuminate ten million;
if he emitted light that passed beyond ten million, it would illuminate a hundred million; if he emitted light that passed beyond a hundred million, it would illuminate a billion.
[The Buddha] said, "Oyi, light is the function of wisdom. This function can adapt to conditions; its magnitude is not fixed, and its breadth or narrowness varies according to the occasion.
It allows for clear vision in all instances and brings awakening to both oneself and others. For example, when threading a needle, [the light] is entirely within the eye of the needle."
One sees everything clearly. When writing characters, one sees them all clearly upon the tip of the brush.
If staying within a single room, one sees everything clearly. If ascending a height to look out, one sees clearly for hundreds or thousands of *li*.
Thus one awakens to the fundamental mind and causes others to know and see it as well.
The "Chapter on the Ten Bodhisattvas’ Questions on Clarification" from the *Jñānālokālaṃkāra-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Arising of Faith through Wisdom’s Illumination):
therein, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī poses questions in prose to the Nine-Headed One, and the Nine-Headed One answers Mañjuśrī in verse.

The Master said: "Inquiry gives rise to clarity; through inquiry within the midst of doubt, clarity arises. Wisdom and clarity give birth to faith, whereby one perceives the emptiness of all phenomena and realizes that the mind is a false movement with no external objects.

By practicing the dharma of detachment, whenever one encounters objects or conditions, one gains self-confidence in one's own nature—that it possesses the Buddha-virtues and the unobstructed dharmas—which are then immediately manifested before one."
Question on the various distinctions within the single mind and the single essence: Answer by Jue-shou (Vijñaptimukha) on the illusory manifestation of the nature of all phenomena.
Question on the non-substantiality of sentient beings and the Buddha’s transformation: Answer by Cai-shou (Dharmodgata) on returning to the nature through the cessation of signs.
Question on who receives retribution if there is no self: Answer by Bao-shou (Ratnamati) on the identity or difference between the image appearing in a mirror and its reflection.
Question on the contradiction between awakening in four ways and teaching in one way: Answer by Guṇamati on the unimpeded mutual establishment of one and many.
Question on the difference between a single field and multiple fruits: Answer by Akṣayamati on the distinction of retribution based on the high and low states of mind.
Question on whether the Buddha’s teachings have benefit or not: Answer by Vīramati on the difference between diligence and indolence.
Question on the new arising of afflictions regarding the seven types of recipients of the Dharma: Dharmottara explains that one does not practice what is improper and refutes excessive learning.
Question on the praise of the assistance of right practice through the eight knowledges: Jñānottara explains that the ten thousand practices all follow the mind of wisdom.
Question on the difference between the single path and the multiple fruits: Bhadrottara explains that there is difference within sameness, free from views.
In nineteen verses, he again questions Mañjuśrī regarding the realm of the Buddha; Mañjuśrī replies that the realm of birth and the dharma-realm are without distinction.
Through this, his wisdom becomes luminous and faith arises. He enters deeply into contemplation of the principle, gains confidence in his own nature, and becomes certain of attaining Buddhahood.
The subsequent arising of pure conduct is near in its manifestation yet far-reaching in its intent; mindfulness is itself non-mindfulness, and in a single thought-moment, it is suddenly perfected.

First, being born into a family of wrong views; second, harboring a mind of deceit and crookedness—by permanently severing these causes, one does not undergo their results.
Third, on the Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākārī*), one initiates ten kinds of profound resolve as the preparatory application (*prayoga*); within the state of entry into the mind, one severs darkness.

Regarding the obstacle of dullness: when realizing the *tathatā* (suchness) of the superior stream within the mind that abides in meditative equipoise, one attains the Buddha-dharma by practicing according to the teachings.

The five sensations arise intermittently; sorrow and suffering are extremely prevalent, while joy, bliss, and equanimity are rare. Anger and desire coexist with the mind, and the mental faculty possesses the sensation of sorrow.
There is no coexistence of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) or the retributive fruit of bliss; if these are cultivated, they do exist. Therefore, it is called the "ground of distraction" (*vikṣepa-bhūmi*). II.

Vicāra (sustained application). It remedies the feeling of sorrow in the desire realm. There are five [factors]: vitarka (applied thought), vicāra, prīti (joy), sukha (bliss), and ekāgratā (one-pointedness of mind).

△ Third, the stage of joyous buoyancy has three [levels]: 1. Ābhāsvara (Radiant); 2. Parittābhā (Limited Radiance); 3. Apramāṇābhā (Immeasurable Radiance). They employ adhyātmasaṃprasāda (internal purity) and ekāgratā.

Fourth, the stage of sublime bliss free from joy (*prītisukhavihāra*) has three [levels]: the Pure (*Śubhakṛtsna*), the Limited-Pure (*Parīttaśubha*), and the Universal-Pure (*Apramāṇaśubha*). These treat the preceding feeling of joy (*prītivedanā*). Internal purity is further divided into equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*);

the correct knowledge consists of the awareness that the body experiences bliss and one-pointedness of mind. Fifth, the stage of pure equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣāsmṛtipariśuddhi*) has three [levels].
1. Anabhraka (Cloudless); 2. Puṇyaprasava (Born of Merit); 3. Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit). These are where ordinary beings and sages dwell together.

Above these are five heavens inhabited exclusively by those who have attained the fruit of Non-returner (Anāgāmin): 1. Avṛha (Without Affliction); 2. Atapa (Without Heat); 3. Sudṛśa (Good Appearance); 4. Sudarśana (Good Vision); 5. Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form).
[They abide in] the equanimity of abandoning mindfulness, the practice of equanimity, and one-pointedness of mind. △ Sixth: the Sphere of Infinite Space; the Two Vehicles and...

Fourth is the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arcismatī-bhūmi*). One observes the realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm as the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) for entering the [main] mind.

In the middle [stage], one severs the afflictive hindrances and realizes the non-appropriated suchness. Abiding within the mind, one contemplates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment with great wisdom.

If one can contemplate the body such that both purity and impurity are found to be unobtainable, one will see that the Buddha never entered parinirvāṇa but dwells eternally in the world. At that very seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because the faculties of sentient beings differ, he further expounded other teachings.

Through each of the four right efforts, the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path, he brought sentient beings to understanding.

The obstacle to the parinirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna; the realization that the categories [of phenomena] are non-different from suchness; the knowledge that the ultimate truth and conventional truth are without distinction;

Sixth is the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*). One contemplates ten kinds of equal dharmas as the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*).

Conditions lack intrinsic nature; from the link of ignorance up to the link of old age and death, all are the light of wisdom.

According to the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), within the contemplation of the distinctions of the marks of truth (*lakṣaṇasatyavibhāga-vipaśyanā*), there is the "Gate of the Succession of the Links" (*aṅgaprabandha-mukha*), which explains the Sūtra.
Answering the characteristics: that all births in the world arise from attachment to a self is the "establishment" (成).

this is the "characteristic" (相). Second is the gate of being subsumed within the one mind: all that exists in the three realms is but the one mind; this is the "return to the source" (歸本). Thus says the Tathāgata.
Within this single mind, the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are distinguished; these are the branches of the flowing [samsaric] process.

The meaning is as follows: that which can induce consists of ignorance and formations; that which is induced consists of the five [factors] beginning with consciousness; that which can produce consists of craving, grasping, and becoming;

and that which is produced consists of birth, old age, and death. Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are the seeds [of these results], which existed in previous lifetimes.

The many thoughts perfuming the lower [consciousness] suddenly become ignorance and formations; gathered together in a single thought, they are moistened first by craving, grasping, and becoming according to whichever karma is strongest.
At the time of this moistening, they arise sequentially within the total retribution of a single lifetime.
These ten links are the cause, and two links are the fruit. If explained according to the three periods of time: the two links of the past are the cause; the five links of the present are the fruit.
The present creates the causes of craving, grasping, and becoming; fundamentally, there are the fruits of birth, aging, and death in the future.
Although cause and fruit are undifferentiated, they manifest before one in this Prajñā.
This is the meaning of the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). It pervades and gives rise to the twelve links and encompasses one hundred dharmas.

One thereby knows the quantity of the five aggregates (*skandha*) and clarifies the breadth or narrowness of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). △ In this single link, the nature is a mixture of both: it encompasses ninety-three dharmas.

Previously, one practiced by means of a single body; now, one practices by means of infinite bodies. Thus...
With skillful wisdom, one contemplates all objects; within the various realms of existence, one manifests forms identical to those beings.
By means of the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting the Physical Body, one preaches the Dharma, remaining far removed from the conceptual discrimination of bodily notions.
Taking the three worlds as the ten bodies, all sentient beings have these inherently from the beginning. If one body possesses nine, then there are ten.
The body has a hundred aspects. For instance, suppose a single ox possesses ten bodies: first, that which repays its debts is the *karmic retribution body*;
second, that which lacks nothing in terms of water and grass is the *sentient-being body*; third, its skin, hair, sinews, and horns is the *land-body*;
fourth, its descending from on high is the *space-body*; fifth, its treading firmly with every step is the *wisdom-body*.
Sixth, being exhausted by the six powers and lying down: this is the body of a śrāvaka. Seventh, seeing yellow leaves: this is the body of a pratyekabuddha.
Eighth, raising the intention to benefit others: this is the body of a bodhisattva. Ninth, suddenly passing away: this is the dharmakāya.

Tenth, possessing all nine [preceding bodies]: this is the body of a Tathāgata. If one speaks in terms of cultivation and accomplishment, these ten are spontaneously possessed within the body of a Tathāgata.
The body refers to the power of adornment through the transformative force of the vow for enlightenment, the mental-born, merit, dharmas, and wisdom.
In this stage, the bodhisattva achieves mastery over the karmic activities of the Buddha-body. A Vajrapāṇi constantly follows and attends him as his guard.
Just as a great jeweled crown made of pure gold is placed upon the head of a noble Cakravartin King of Jambudvīpa, [the Bodhisattva] frequently becomes a Great Brahmā King.

On the ninth stage, the Ground of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī*), he takes the observation of the objective sphere through immeasurable wisdom as his preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) for entering [the path].
Within the mind, one severs the obstacle of non-willingness to practice within the gateway of benefiting others. One realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) of mastery over wisdom.
While abiding in this state of mind, one observes the conduct of the dense forest of sentient beings and knows it all as it truly is.
By means of forty kinds of eloquence, one expounds the Dharma of the three vehicles to teach and transform sentient beings.
The commentary states: "In the mind it is wisdom (*jñāna*); when expressed in speech it is eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

To possess forty kinds of eloquence within a single hair-tip means that the former constitutes the "Dharma to be realized" (*deśya-dharma*), while the latter constitutes the "meaning to be realized" (*artha*). "Words" (*pada*) refers to the unerring explanation of definitions;

"joyful speech" (*pratibhāna*) refers to the listener’s attainment of understanding and liberation. Part One: Self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) has two aspects: the general nature of phenomena (*dharmasāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and their specific meanings (*paryāya-artha*).

△ Second, the characteristic of sameness has two aspects: 1) the meaning of the nature of phenomena (dharmasvabhāva), and 2) the characteristic of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa). △ Third, the characteristic of activity has two aspects: 1) present phenomena, and 2) the meaning of past phenomena.

△ Fourth, the characteristic of exposition has two aspects: 1) brief exposition of phenomena, and 2) the meaning of understanding through explanation. △ Fifth, the characteristic of knowledge has two aspects:

1) direct perception of phenomena (pratyakṣa-dharma), and 2) the meaning of inferential cognition (anumāna-jñāna). △ Sixth, the characteristic of truth has two aspects: 1) ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and 2) conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

The Buddha taught that all one hundred dharmas are fully present; all myriad phenomena are fully present. One knows them without learning; yet, though one has heard their words, one has not yet seen them.

this constitutes the mind of application (*prayoga-citta*). Within the mind of entry, he attains the Samādhi Free from Defilement (*vimala-samādhi*) and severs that which has not yet been attained regarding the dharmas.

When the Bodhisattva sits upon this flower, the proportions of body and seat are perfectly harmonious. From all the pores of his body, he universally emits rays of light that illuminate the entire Dharma-realm;

The phenomena being illustrated are the pond, the mountain, the ocean, and the jewel; these serve as the bases for the illustration. The meaning based upon them is the "reflection.
This reflection of the earth represents the scriptural and logical proofs found within the section on the earth. The pond illustrates the vows of the practices undertaken;
the mountain illustrates the merits accomplished through cultivation; the ocean illustrates the merit of untainted wisdom; and the jewel [illustrates the ultimate fruit].
These metaphors illustrate the nature of the transformation and the exhaustion of inherent virtues. The pond metaphor signifies that which is neither identical nor different at the beginning and end.
The mountain metaphor signifies that the supported (the phenomena) are not one, while the support (the ground) is not different. In all these cases above, there is difference within non-difference.

The ocean metaphor signifies that the ten virtues are distinct, yet these virtues have no separate substance; difference is itself non-difference. The jewel metaphor signifies that the single nature of wisdom increases progressively from beginning to end.
Ming [states]: "Non-differentiation does not obstruct differentiation. 'The pond' represents the gradual within the Perfect; 'the mountain' represents the gradual within the Middle of the Perfect;

the pearl is a metaphor for the gradual-perfect; the ocean is a metaphor for the perfect-perfect. Tiantai takes the *Avataṃsaka* as the gradual-perfect, wherein Buddhahood is attained at every stage."

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the "perfect-perfect" (*yuanyuanyuan*). The former is the perfection of the Dharma, as it does not speak of stages (*bhūmi*). The latter is the perfection for those of inferior capacity, as it universally benefits the śrāvakas.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* takes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* as its gradual perfection, for it brings the three vehicles back to the great ocean of the one vehicle.
In the original teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition—this is the "superior perfection"; the fruition penetrates to the source of the cause.

7. The samādhi of the adornment of all buddha-worlds in the present.
